extracted.intended_audience: combinatorics researchers, potential authors/editors, and librarians interested in ethical/open-access journal options
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what the new journal Advances in Combinatorics will accept and on starting/choosing ethical open-access combinatorics journals; useful for authors deciding where to submit and for people thinking of launching community-run journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal scope (subject focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advances in Combinatorics is set up as a combinatorics journal for high-quality papers, principally in the less algebraic parts of combinatorics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consider the journal if their work fits the less algebraic side of combinatorics and aims at a specialist combinatorics readership. The journal complements other outlets (e.g., Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, Algebraic Combinatorics) by focusing on this subarea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access / no author charges (diamond OA)
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be an arXiv overlay journal, so free to read, and it will not charge authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal operates as a diamond-open-access model: readers have free access and authors pay no APCs. Financial support is provided by a supporting library (Queen’s University Library) and minimal platform costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: arXiv-overlay / preprint requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles under consideration will already be in the public domain, since it is a requirement of the journal that they should be posted to arXiv. (Later wording changed to 'publicly available'.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should already be posted as preprints (on the arXiv or equivalent) before consideration; the overlay model uses those preprints as the version-of-record for hosting and linking. Authors should ensure their preprint is publicly accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial-board engagement and workload expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: All members of the editorial board will be expected to work: they won’t just be lending their names to give the journal bogus prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should actively handle papers; membership implies commitment to real editorial duties rather than honorary listing. Work should be distributed reasonably uniformly among board members where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling and decision-making process
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paper will be handled by one of the editors, who, after obtaining external opinions (when the paper warrants them) will make a recommendation to the rest of the board. All decisions will be made collectively. The job of the managing editors will be to make sure that this process runs smoothly, but when it comes to decisions, they will have no more say than any other editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers get an assigned editor; external reviews are solicited as needed; decisions follow from board discussion and collective vote/recommendation; managing editors coordinate but do not overrule others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target standard / quality level
rubrics_metrics.description: The rough level that the journal is aiming at is that of a top specialist journal such as Combinatorica.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal aims to be a top specialist venue — authors should expect selectivity comparable to established specialist journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: High acceptance bar / low acceptance volume
rubrics_metrics.description: We plan to set a higher bar for acceptance, even if it means that we accept only a small number of papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the journal is electronic and not constrained by fixed issue sizes, standards will not be artificially lowered to fill issues; expect selective acceptance and a focus on quality over quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a 'pretty good' paper (what to submit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work in a good paper should have a clear reason for others to be interested in it (so not, for example, incremental progress in some pet project of the author) and should have something about it that makes it count as a significant achievement, such as solving a well-known problem, clearing a difficult technical hurdle, inventing a new and potentially useful technique, or giving a beautiful and memorable proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid submitting narrowly incremental results; desirable contributions include problem solutions, major technical advances, new techniques with potential broader use, or particularly elegant proofs. This gives concrete signals of what the editorial board will value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical criteria for journals (publisher and access model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason for setting it up is that there is a gap in the market for an 'ethical' combinatorics journal at that level — that is, one that is not published by one of the major commercial publishers, with all the well known problems that result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'ethical' journal in this context means non-commercial or nonprofit publishing, transparency on costs, not complicit in exploitative 'big deals', and providing free access to readers without charging authors where possible. Authors who prioritize these values should consider such journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/operational viability and minimal costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Its minimal costs are being paid for by the library at Queen’s University in Ontario, which is also providing administrative support... the total cost of running a new journal that isn’t too large is of the order of a few hundred dollars per year, as long as nobody is paid for what they do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting/maintaining small community journals is affordable with modest library support and platform choices; platform fees (e.g., Scholastica submission fee $10) and CrossRef DOI subscriptions are modest recurring costs. Large-scale (higher-volume) journals require more funding and organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform choices for running a journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating the journal itself can be done on one of a number of different platforms, either for no charge or for a very small charge. Some examples are the Mersenne platform, the Episciences platform, and Scholastica. Of these, Scholastica charges a submission fee of $10 per article and the other two are free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When starting a journal, consider overlay-hosting platforms (Mersenne, Episciences) or platforms like Scholastica depending on budget and feature needs; account for DOI registration and other small recurring fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use honorary/ghost editorial lists
rubrics_metrics.description: I’m also not very comfortable with the practice of having a long list of names of editors, most of whom have zero involvement in the decisions of the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial boards should reflect actual contributors; avoid listing many honorary editors who do not participate in editorial work, as this misrepresents the journal's governance and may undermine trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of libraries and funding options for community journals
rubrics_metrics.description: There are almost certainly other libraries that would be interested in following the enlightened example of Queen’s University Library and supporting a journal (if you are a librarian reading this, then I strongly recommend doing so)... I can offer advice, funding (if the proposal looks a good one), and contact with several other people who are knowledgeable and keen to help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community journals can be funded by library support, small grants, or consortia; potential founders should solicit library partners and other non-profit funders rather than relying on APC models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of electronic/overlay model for maintaining standards
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the great advantages of a fully electronic journal is that we do not have a fixed number of issues per year, so we will not have to change our standards artificially in order to fill issues or clear backlogs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic continuous-publishing removes pressure to accept papers merely to fill issues, enabling consistently high standards and rapid publication when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community involvement in editor selection (recommended practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: When expanding the editorial board, some community input be solicited. The model used by Quantum, where a steering committee makes a public call for nominations for editors, seems reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public calls, steering committees, and community nominations increase community buy-in and transparency in editorial appointments; consider these methods rather than closed appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Niche/tier coverage question (journals needed at different levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a gap... for the next tier of papers... some ethical journals set a very high standard and publish too few pages to serve as a replacement for journals at the next tier down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and founders should consider the need for journals at multiple tiers (top, second-tier, moderate) to serve career needs across institutions; founding initiatives should weigh whether they target high-selectivity small-volume journals or larger mid-tier outlets with greater capacity.
